title: Standard method for microCT-based additive manufacturing quality control 2: Density measurement
author: du Plessis, Sperling, et al.

steps.title: Build coupon samples by SLM
steps.instruction: Manufacture 10 × 10 × 10 mm Ti6Al4V cubes on a custom selective laser melting (SLM) platform inside a commercial LENS enclosure using an IPG YLS 5000 ytterbium fibre laser (5 kW, 1076 nm wavelength, 50 µm core). Use an Intelliweld 30 FC V scanner. Feedstock: gas‑atomized Ti6Al4V (particle size 20–60 µm, supplied by TLS Technik GmbH). Set hatch parameters to 3 kW power, 3 m s⁻¹ speed, 240 µm spot size. For contour scans use 1 kW laser power; vary hatch‑contour distance and speed as required to study density effects. Base plate: Ti6Al4V, 150 mm diameter, ~40 mm thick.

steps.title: Select standard coupon size
steps.instruction: Use a 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm (cube) coupon for the density test; no additional sample preparation is required.

steps.title: Mount sample in foam
steps.instruction: Place the cube in low‑density foam at an angle (to avoid edge artifacts) as illustrated in the first paper of this series.

steps.title: Acquire microCT scan
steps.instruction: Scan the mounted sample on a standard laboratory microCT system with the following settings: 200 kV, 70 µA, 0.5 mm beam filter, voxel size ≈15 µm, 500 ms exposure per image, 2400 projection steps over a full 360 ° rotation. At each step discard the first image and average the next two images. Total acquisition time is just under 1 h; including sample setup, machine warm‑up, background correction and reconstruction the whole process should be ≤2 h.

steps.title: Reconstruct CT data
steps.instruction: Reconstruct the raw projections using a strong beam‑hardening correction factor; do not apply any image de‑noising.

steps.title: Segment part and determine volume
steps.instruction: Process the reconstructed volume in Volume Graphics VGStudioMax 3.1 to obtain an unbiased total part volume:

substeps.instruction: Create a region of interest (ROI) from the detected surface.
Apply an opening/closing morphological operation with a value of +3 to close small surface pores.
Run the region‑growing tool with high tolerance (ignoring grey‑value differences) and select the option “avoid other visible ROIs” to label all exterior air up to the part surface.
If loose powder or noise particles are present outside the part, apply another opening/closing (+3) to the exterior‑air region to remove them.
Invert the exterior‑air selection; the resulting selection now contains the entire part, including closed internal voids.
Apply the advanced surface determination function using the inverted ROI as the starting contour; this yields sub‑voxel‑precise surface geometry.
Read the total object volume from the Properties tab.

steps.title: Calculate mean density
steps.instruction: Measure the mass of the same coupon (e.g., with an analytical balance) and divide by the volume obtained in the previous step to obtain the mean density of the part.

description: Additive manufacturing is a fast growing manufacturing method especially useful for medical and aerospace applications, due to the complexity of design that is possible. Various efforts at qualification of systems and materials for different applications are in process, such as demonstrated for medical applications in [1]. There is a need for standardization in quality inspections especially for microCT but more generally for all NDT methods [2]. Part density is usually measured by the Archimedes method [3], which is a standardized and very accurate method. However, this method does have some drawbacks: it requires an assumption of the parent material density, which can potentially be incorrect for alloys depending on the content of different atomic elements. The second drawback is the possibility for surface roughness to capture bubbles and hence measure a higher volume than expected, while small channels connected to the surface may lead into larger cavities, where the water (or gas) will penetrate the sample and hence a smaller volume recorded, and this may not be visible to the human eye. Unconsolidated powder trapped inside cavities or pores will also result in lower density by Archimedes but not significantly so (due to the mass of the powder), and the presence of a large cavity with unconsolidated powder may be missed or not realized. While the use of microCT for analysis of porosity is well known (see for example [4]), it is not so well known that accurate material volumes can be determined, which can be used indirectly to calculate a mean density for samples. This is an entirely different approach than measuring porosity, and can be useful when some pores may be smaller than the voxel size, or when the alloy density might be incorrect. In this work we demonstrate a simple methodology where no sample preparation is required – a simple 10 mm coupon sample (cube) is required. The scan method and analysis workflow makes use of commercial hardware and software,
